01.r: Continues the description of the believers from the previous verse.

02.r: The article, which here points to the believers' own possessions.
02.n: Greek often uses the article where English uses a possessive; the YLT keeps 'the'.

03.r: What they owned, very likely including land.
03.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from κτάομαι, to acquire, and gives 'a possession, property'; he notes the Septuagint uses it for כֶּרֶם, a vineyard. That this word means land and the next means movable goods is a common reading and an inference; the verse does not draw the line.

04.r: Joins the two kinds of property.

05.r: A second article, which keeps the goods a category of their own.

06.r: Their other property and means of living.
06.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from ὑπάρχω; its first sense is 'subsistence, existence', and in late writers 'substance, property'. He cites this verse for the plural.

07.r: They sold their property, again and again as it was needed.
07.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to sell', with the thing sold as object, and he cites this verse. An imperfect: a repeated practice, not one sale. Abbott-Smith also records the verb of selling persons into slavery.

08.r: Joins the selling to the sharing out.

09.r: They shared out the proceeds among the believers.
09.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to distribute', with the people receiving in the dative, and he cites this verse. Also an imperfect: they kept on distributing. The KJV's 'parted' is the older sense of part, to divide.

10.r: The things sold, or what they fetched.
10.n: The pronoun points back to the possessions and goods; what was shared out was presumably the money they brought, an inference from the selling.

11.r: Among all the believers, as the next phrase limits it: to those in need.

12.r: The measure of the sharing was each one's need.
12.n: Abbott-Smith: 'according as, just as', with this verse cited. In late Greek the same word can also mean 'because', a sense that does not fit here.

13.r: A particle that makes the clause general: whenever anyone had need.
13.n: Abbott-Smith says this particle cannot usually be translated on its own in English; its force depends on its construction. Here, with a past tense, it marks something that happened again and again, so it has no English word of its own.

14.r: Any believer at all who was in want.

15.r: Real lack, which set the measure of the gift.

16.r: Each case of need as it arose.
